lines.speaker: Agamemnon
lines.text: If, in your madness, Ajax, you killed yourself—and very nearly all of us as well—why blame Odysseus? The other day, when he came up to consult the oracle, you would not even look at him. You did not think a fellow-soldier and comrade worth a word. You just swept past him, taking those enormous strides of yours.

lines.speaker: Ajax
lines.text: With good reason, Agamemnon. He was the cause of my madness. He alone stood against me in the contest for the armour.

lines.speaker: Agamemnon
lines.text: And you expected to have no opponent? To win the whole thing without raising dust?

lines.speaker: Ajax
lines.text: Yes. In a case like that, yes. The armour was family property: it belonged to my cousin. And the rest of you—better men than he was, by a long way—declined the contest and made room for me. But Laertes' son, whom I saved again and again when the Phrygians were about to cut him to pieces, decided he was the better man, and more fit to own the armour.

lines.speaker: Agamemnon
lines.text: Then blame Thetis, my noble friend. She ought to have handed the inheritance over to you, as the kinsman. Instead she brought the armour in and put it before the whole army.

lines.speaker: Ajax
lines.text: No. Odysseus. He was the only one who made a claim.

lines.speaker: Agamemnon
lines.text: Forgive him, Ajax. He was human; he wanted glory—the sweetest thing there is, the thing every one of us went through danger for. And, after all, he beat you. With Trojans as the judges, too.

lines.speaker: Ajax
lines.text: I know who condemned me. But it is not lawful to say anything about the gods. As for Odysseus, Agamemnon, I could not stop hating him. Not even if Athena herself ordered me to.
